# Getting On The Net
This page walks you from spawning in to having a working conversation over the radio.
It assumes you have never used the communications system before. Follow the steps in order and you should be on the net without needing to understand the rest of the radio system first.
If something still refuses to work, see [bold]When it does not work[/bold] near the end.
## Step 1: Check what you have
Most roles spawn wearing a [bold]field headset[/bold] in the ears slot.
This is your personal radio and, for most roles, it is the only radio equipment you need.
CLF characters use a concealable earpiece clipped into their clothing instead. It works in much the same way, but does not appear in an ears slot. See [textlink="Field Headsets" link="AU14CommsHeadsets"] for the differences.
Some roles also spawn with an [bold]AN/PRC-117G[/bold] manpack radio in their back slot.
The manpack does more than let you transmit. It also provides radio coverage for nearby headsets.
Check your inventory before going any further:
- [bold]Headset only[/bold] - read steps 2 and 3, then continue to the handset section if you need access to another net. - [bold]Headset and manpack[/bold] - read the full guide. You are carrying one of the radios that keeps nearby combat nets working.
## Step 2: Understand relay coverage
This is the most important thing to understand about combat radio.
Your headset does [bold]not[/bold] reach across the map by itself.
Combat nets are [bold]relay-gated[/bold]. Your headset only works while you are within range of something carrying that net.
A net can be anchored by:
- a powered AN/PRC worn by a trained operator - a deployed retransmission station - a command-post antenna mast - a powered shipboard communications array - a vehicle radio aboard a dropship or other vehicle - a field antenna mast raised by engineering-trained personnel - a CLF clandestine base station - a staked CLF relay set - a mast or array carrying a CLF splice
If there is no suitable anchor in range, your combat net does not work.
You can speak into the headset normally, but nothing will be transmitted.
This is why staying within range of your squad's radio matters. In many squads, that radio is carried by the [bold]Fireteam Leader[/bold].
Colony and civilian channels are different. They are not relay-gated and can be used without nearby relay coverage.
They are also not private.
### How far is "in range"?
[bold]Distance from the anchor[/bold]
[bold]What you get[/bold]
0-30 tiles
Clear traffic in both directions.
30-45 tiles
Degraded but usually readable traffic. Some words may be lost.
Beyond 45 tiles
No connection.
Coverage normally reaches one level above and below the anchor.
Tunnels, lower decks, and other vertically separated areas may therefore need their own relay.
Shipboard communications arrays are the exception and can cover an entire site vertically.
### If you are with the CLF
The CLF do not have a permanent communications array.
Their radio coverage comes from equipment they deploy themselves, or from enemy infrastructure they successfully tap.
A cell starts with a manpack, a base station, a splice kit, and two relay sets. These are drawn by the Cell Leader or Radio Operator, depending on who is present.
The issued manpack begins already tuned to the cell net and cell command, so it works as soon as somebody wears it.
Additional equipment can be built at the sapper's workbench or purchased through Special Equipment.
#### Tapping another mast
Fixed communications masts and arrays have feeder junctions that can be spliced.
A successful splice adds your cell nets to that structure's existing coverage.
A command-post mast gives your nets 75 tiles of coverage. A site array gives them 200.
Field antenna masts work differently.
They only carry nets belonging to sides whose COMSEC key has been loaded into the mast.
If the garrison built the mast, you must first [bold]key it for your own side[/bold]:
1. Open the feed with a screwdriver, then wirecutters. The mast goes off the air while the feed is open. 2. Use your fill card on the feed. 3. Close the feed with a screwdriver and seal it with a welder.
This requires engineering training and the appropriate tools.
Using a multitool on an open feed wipes the existing stored keys.
A splice [bold]adds[/bold] your nets. It does not remove the nets already carried by the mast.
Splicing a garrison mast therefore does not disable, jam, or otherwise interfere with its original radio coverage.
To splice a fixed mast or array, you need a [bold]net splice kit[/bold] and must be playing the [bold]Radio Operator[/bold].
Use the kit on the mast. After the cover is removed, the splice panel opens.
The panel hides several trunk carriers across the band. Your job is to locate each one.
- [bold]PROBE[/bold] checks a position in the band. Stronger readings mean you are closer to a carrier. A result of zero means there is no carrier within thirty positions of the point you checked. - [bold]LOCK[/bold] attempts to capture the carrier. If your guess is within three positions, the lock succeeds. - Missing a lock consumes two probes and adds a large amount to the detection meter. - Probes are shared across the whole splice attempt.
It is safer to narrow a carrier down with probes than to guess repeatedly.
A coarse sweep across the band can give you a starting point, after which you can move toward the strongest response.
If you run out of probes or fill the detection meter, the splice fails.
The kit is consumed and the junction enters a fault state for ninety seconds. During that time, nobody can attempt another splice.
The mast also sparks while you are working on it, including during the fault state, so the attempt is visibly noticeable.
#### Building your own coverage
CLF can also establish their own relay network.
- A [bold]field antenna mast[/bold] costs ten metal sheets, takes eight seconds to raise, and provides 75 tiles of clear coverage with degraded traffic out to 100. Cell Leaders, Radio Operators, Guerillas, and Machine Gunners have the engineering skill to build one. Field masts must be placed outdoors and can be damaged or tapped by either side. - A [bold]clandestine base station[/bold] provides 55 tiles of clear coverage and degraded traffic out to 80. It also has a usable handset. The station is too heavy to conceal on a person. - A [bold]relay set[/bold] provides 35 tiles of clear coverage and degraded traffic out to 50. It has no local controls and is mainly useful where a mast cannot be raised, such as inside buildings or tunnels.
Only the Cell Leader and Radio Operator can stake down a relay or base station.
#### Protecting CLF relay equipment
CLF communications equipment is not hidden automatically.
A [bold]splice[/bold] remains visible at the base of the mast.
It can be shot or removed by somebody standing beside it. Removing it takes eight seconds and gives the person the splice's keying module.
That module can read your cell's traffic until your leadership performs a recrypto.
A [bold]relay set[/bold] is also only staked into place.
Anybody can pack it up in about three seconds and carry it away.
Consider where you place either one, especially if enemy personnel regularly move through the area.
## Step 3: Use your headset
With your headset equipped, type:
[color=#a4885c]:h Radio check, over.[/color]
The important part is:
[color=#a4885c]:h[/color]
This sends the following message over the headset's default radio net.
If the net has relay coverage and somebody else is listening, they will see your callsign followed by your message.
Your headset may contain more than one net.
Examine it to see which channel prefixes are available.
Common examples include:
- [color=#a4885c]:v[/color] for command, if your headset contains the command key - [color=#a4885c]:a[/color] for Alpha, if your headset contains the Alpha key
A headset cannot use a net unless it contains the appropriate key.
Headset keys cannot normally be added in the field.
Your [bold]character name is not transmitted over radio[/bold].
Other listeners see your callsign instead, whether they are friendly or hostile.
Normal face-to-face speech is unchanged.
## Step 4: Open the manpack
Everything from this point requires an AN/PRC-117G and radio-operator training.
The following roles begin trained:
[bold]Faction[/bold]
[bold]Trained roles[/bold]
[bold]GOVFOR and OPFOR[/bold]
Commander, Adjutant, staff officers, engineering officers, intelligence officers, synthetics, squad leaders, Fireteam Leaders, and Radio Traffic Operators.
[bold]CLF[/bold]
Cell Leader and Radio Operator.
GOVFOR and OPFOR use the same training requirements, so somebody trained to operate one side's AN/PRC can also operate a captured set from the other.
If you are not trained, you cannot open the radio panel or transmit directly through the pack.
You can still:
- use somebody else's handset - read a [bold]field radio operator's pamphlet[/bold], if one is available, to gain the training permanently
To open the panel:
1. Wear the AN/PRC in your [bold]back slot[/bold]. 2. Alt-click the radio, or open its verb menu. 3. Select [bold]Open Radio Panel[/bold].
The radio must be worn. A pack sitting in your hands, inside a bag, or on the floor does not operate as a worn manpack.
The first time you open the panel, a short briefing appears.
The [bold]? HELP[/bold] button at the top of the panel opens it again later.
Below the radio display is a status banner.
If something prevents normal operation, the banner tells you what needs attention and usually provides a button to fix it.
When the banner turns green, the radio is ready.
## Step 5: Load your nets
A worn AN/PRC relays every friendly combat net stored in its memory.
This means the nets you load affect not only you, but nearby headset users.
The quickest way to set up a fresh radio is:
- Press [bold]LOAD STANDARD NETS[/bold] on the status banner or NETS tab.
This:
- switches the radio on - loads your squad net - loads your side's command net - selects your squad net as the active transmission net
It only fills available memory slots and does not overwrite memories you tuned yourself.
It also leaves your current operating mode, encryption state, and power settings unchanged.
### Loading a net manually
On the [bold]NETS[/bold] tab:
1. Select [bold]+ ADD MEMORY[/bold]. 2. Give the memory a short label, such as [bold]CMD[/bold]. 3. Select [bold]EDIT[/bold]. 4. Choose the net you want from the list. 5. Select [bold]USE[/bold] if you want to transmit on that memory.
Your squad net is marked [bold][YOUR SQUAD][/bold].
The memory currently selected for transmission is marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold].
Loading a net does not automatically make it active.
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] always transmits through the memory marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold].
The memory editor can also rename, empty, or delete memories.
Direct frequencies are configured through the expert faceplate.
## Step 6: Load your COMSEC fill
Most faction radio traffic is intended to be encrypted.
The AN/PRC does not store its own faction key permanently. Instead, it reads the key from a physical [bold]fill card[/bold].
To load one:
1. Find the issued fill card in your equipment. 2. Use it on the radio. 3. Open the [bold]SECURITY[/bold] tab. 4. Check that the radio reads [bold]ENCRYPTED[/bold].
If you transmit over a secured faction net without the matching fill, the radio does [bold]not[/bold] stop you.
It warns you, then sends the traffic in the clear.
Anyone capable of receiving that frequency can read it, and the transmission also creates a direction-finding signature.
If the radio warns you about the fill, check the SECURITY tab before continuing.
## Step 7: Transmit through the manpack
Once the radio has an active memory, use:
[color=#a4885c]:r HAVOC 6, this is ALPHA ROMEO, radio check, over.[/color]
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] transmits through whichever memory is currently marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold].
The TALK line on the radio display also shows where your message will go.
If you need another net, switch to that memory before transmitting.
A worn radio normally uses the [bold]wearer's assigned callsign[/bold].
The guided panel shows this as [bold]AUTO[/bold].
If you do not currently have a callsign assigned, the radio identifies you as [bold]UNKNOWN STATION[/bold].
## Step 8: Check the link
The radio includes a built-in [bold]RADIO CHECK[/bold].
Using it sends:
[bold]RADIO CHECK, HOW COPY, OVER[/bold]
over the active net.
The radio then privately reports which stations received the check and whether each received it clearly or degraded.
This includes ordinary headset and earpiece users, not only other AN/PRC operators.
RADIO CHECK is therefore useful when you want to confirm whether the net has working coverage without waiting for somebody else to answer manually.
If you perform a radio check while inside an enemy jammer field, the report also gives you a rough bearing toward the strongest jammer.
## The handset
The handset lets somebody use an AN/PRC without needing radio-operator training.
It is particularly useful when someone needs access to a net their own headset does not carry.
To take the handset:
1. Stand within roughly [bold]two and a half tiles[/bold] of the radio or its wearer. 2. Make sure you have a [bold]free hand[/bold]. 3. Alt-click the wearer or deployed radio. 4. Select [bold]Take Handset[/bold].
[bold]While you are holding the handset, normal speech is transmitted over the radio.[/bold]
You do not need to type a radio prefix.
This also means that ordinary conversation can accidentally go over the net while you are holding it.
Use [bold]whisper[/bold] when you want to speak locally without transmitting.
The handset also follows these rules:
- It transmits over the radio's currently active memory. - It uses [bold]your callsign[/bold], not the radio operator's. - Only one person can hold it at a time. - Moving beyond the cord's range causes the handset to snap back and disconnect. - Select [bold]Hang Up Handset[/bold] to return it.
If you are wearing your own AN/PRC while holding somebody else's handset, your own manpack takes priority.
In that case, normal [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] operation applies instead of the borrowed handset opening your microphone.
## When it does not work
If your radio is not behaving as expected, check these common problems.
[bold]Symptom[/bold]
[bold]Check[/bold]
Nobody answers on a squad or command net
You may be outside relay coverage. Move closer to your squad's radio, a mast, or another suitable anchor.
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] goes out on the wrong net
Check which memory is marked ON AIR and select the correct one with USE.
The radio panel will not open
Check that the radio is in your back slot and that your character has radio-operator training.
Traffic is broken or full of static
You may be near the edge of relay coverage or inside a jammer field. Moving closer to the relay may improve the signal.
AN/PRC traffic arrives as pure static
The transmitting and receiving radios may not have matching COMSEC fills.
Your headset is missing a net
Examine the headset and check its installed keys. Headset keys cannot normally be added in the field; use a handset if you need access to another net.
You transmit as UNKNOWN STATION
No callsign is currently assigned to you. Command can assign one through the net directory.
Something private went out over the radio
You are probably holding a handset. Hang it up, or whisper when speaking locally.
The AN/PRC has stopped working entirely
Check the power cell in its dedicated slot. Searching and high output power drain the battery more quickly.
